The study identified the five most important activities for vocational special needs educators (VSNEs).

The five most important activities were: acting as an advocate for students, communicating with involved parties, participating in the development of individualized plans, using assessment results to develop individualized plans, and providing instruction on employability skills.
Cluster analysis revealed 8 clusters of activities, with two main clusters being 'communicating' and 'conducting career preparation activities.'
The study used a descriptive survey design with a questionnaire containing 44 Likert-scale items.
Participants included 264 Special Populations Coordinators (SPCs) from North Carolina and 37 national experts in vocational special needs education.
The overall response rate was 69.77%.
The questionnaire had a very high degree of internal consistency, with a split-half reliability of r = +.94 after correction.
The theoretical framework was based on the organizational analysis model from Rummler and Brache.

The five broad functions of SPCs according to North Carolina's Department of Public Instruction are: outreach and recruitment, assessment/prescription, coordination with other service providers, monitoring access, progress, and success, and annual accountability/planning.
A clear job description is important for SPCs to set goals, self-evaluate, and receive feedback from supervisors.
The study used a snowball sampling process to select the expert panel.
The study provided recommendations for developing a clear and justified job description for SPCs.
The study's findings can inform the structure of job descriptions and training programs for SPCs.

Key legislation influencing vocational special needs education includes the Vocational Education Act of 1963, the Education for All Handicapped Children Act of 1975, the Carl D. Perkins Vocational Education Act of 1984, and the School-to-Work Opportunities Act of 1994.
